meta.description: Not Eleanor Roosevelt. Quote Investigator traces the line to a 1932 book, Human Engineering, where a foreman says it. Roosevelt is not credited until 2000.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You must learn from the mistakes of others. You can't possibly live long enough to make them all yourself'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous shop-floor saying, in print by 1932 and pinned on Eleanor Roosevelt only around 2000. The documented chronology, sourced.

answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — an anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: First close match in print, 1932 · originator unidentified
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the first close match to the 1932 book Human Engineering, where the line is put in the mouth of an unnamed foreman addressing a young worker called William. Eleanor Roosevelt’s name was not attached to it in the record QI assembled until a newspaper item in 2000 — long after the saying was circulating as anonymous folk wisdom.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the saying predates the Roosevelt credit by decades and no source ties it to her.

source.heading: Where the line actually first appears

docMeta.dd: An unnamed foreman, speaking to a young worker called William
Not until 2000 in the record assembled by Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: William, you must learn from the mistakes of others—you will never live long enough to make them all yourself.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ identifies the first close match in the 1932 book Human Engineering by Harry Myers and Mason M. Roberts, where a foreman tells a worker named William the line.

Precursors run much earlier in QI’s chronology — an 1837 Evening Post item tentatively linked to Benjamin Franklin, then anonymous newspaper versions in 1901, 1902, 1905 and 1918, with American Machinist in 1920 already using “making them all yourself” ↗.
Wikiquote places the saying in its Disputed section for Eleanor Roosevelt ↗, describing it as anonymous folk-wisdom from the 1940s onward that was not attributed to her until 2001.
The book itself is catalogued at Open Library ↗ as Human Engineering, Harry Myers, Harper & Brothers, New York, 1932, 318 pages, LCCN 32026248.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 1932 book Human Engineering. The familiar modern form — “you can’t live long enough” — appears in newspapers from the 1940s; the “can’t possibly” variant is a later smoothing of the same sentence.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording. The saying is an evolved, anonymous one with no identified author, so there is no rights holder to name — and the earliest book to carry the close match, Human Engineering, was published in 1932, which in the United States is past the automatic public-domain cutoff (currently 1930); whether it is still in copyright depends on a 28th-year renewal we have not verified. Quotle.info therefore treats the status as undetermined and quotes only the short passage under discussion.

author.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
author.heading: About Eleanor Roosevelt
author.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt wrote prolifically — the Eleanor Roosevelt Papers Project counts roughly 8,000 “My Day” newspaper columns, 27 books and 1,000 speeches among her output — which is precisely why unattributed aphorisms drift toward her name. This particular saying is not among her documented writings. It was already in print as anonymous shop-floor wisdom while she was in the White House, and the credit to her surfaces only around the turn of the twenty-first century.

misattribution.heading: Everyone has been given credit for this one
misattribution.intro: The saying has been reassigned repeatedly. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows each of these names attaching to it after the line was already circulating in print.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s earliest Roosevelt citation is an item in the Albany Democrat-Herald in 2000; Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗, noting it was cited as anonymous folk-wisdom from the 1940s onward and not attributed to her until 2001.
QI records the saying in 1983 coverage of a Rickover speech ↗ before the California Democratic Council — decades after it was in print.
Credited in the Port Huron Times Herald in 1995 ↗, per QI’s chronology.
Attached to Holmes in the Honolulu Star-Advertiser in 2012 ↗ — the most recent reassignment QI logs.
An early named credit: QI dates it to the Trenton Evening Times in 1951 ↗ and treats it, like the others, as a linkage formed after the saying was in circulation.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: the saying evolved over time and the originator remains anonymous.

context.heading: A shop-floor joke that kept changing hands
lead: The saying has the shape of workplace advice because that is where it seems to have lived first. Quote Investigator’s chronology runs through trade and small-town papers — a 1902 item in the Topeka State Journal, a 1905 piece in the Falls City Tribune, a 1920 appearance in American Machinist that already uses the distinctive tail “making them all yourself” — before the fully modern sentence surfaces in the 1932 book Human Engineering.

Because it was nobody’s in particular, it became everybody’s. QI records the line being handed to Martin Vanbee in 1951, to Admiral Hyman Rickover after a 1983 speech, to Sam Levenson in 1995, to Eleanor Roosevelt in 2000 and to Oliver Wendell Holmes in 2012 — each credit landing well after the saying was already in circulation.
context.pull: An anonymous foreman’s line, reassigned to a new celebrity roughly once a decade.
